Time has always been one of Christopher Nolan’s biggest obsessions. Not simply time travel, but the way we experience time, remember it, lose it and sometimes fight against it. Across his films, time is rarely just part of the story. It often becomes the story itself.⁣
⁣
In 𝐌𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨, Nolan tells the story backwards, placing us inside the mind of a man who cannot form new memories. 𝐈𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 explores how time moves at different speeds across layers of dreams. In 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐫, relativity turns minutes for one character into years for another, making time the film’s most painful obstacle. 𝐃𝐮𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐫𝐤 tells three connected stories taking place across a week, a day and a single hour. And in 𝐓𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐭, Nolan pushes the idea even further by allowing events to move both forwards and backwards through time.⁣
⁣
What interests Nolan is that time is something everyone understands but nobody can control. We constantly move through it, yet our perception of it changes depending on what we are experiencing. An hour can disappear in seconds or feel endless.⁣
⁣
That gives Nolan the perfect filmmaking tool. By manipulating time, he can change how we understand a story while also exploring memory, ageing, regret and loss. For Nolan, time isn’t just a concept. It’s perhaps the most important character in his movies.
